newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Democrats lean toward opposition status.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Democrats lean toward opposition status.

text.p: Japan's reformist Democratic Party on Wednesday signalled its intent to battle for change from the opposition benches rather than join any new coalition led by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
In Sunday's general election, Hashimoto's conservative Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) fell 12 seats short of the 251 seats it needs for a majority in the powerful Lower House.

It has therefore been courting its partners in the outgoing coalition, the Social Democrats and the tiny Sakigake Party, and eyeing an alliance with the fledgling Democrats, who have the third-largest block of seats in the Lower House.
"Now is the time for us to hunker down," Yukio Hatoyama, co-leader of the Democratic Party told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
"No decision has been made since we have not yet been officially approached by the LDP, but basically, I believe that our stance should be to start off as an opposition party."
The Democrats, created just before the election by Sakigake and Social Democrat defectors, won 52 seats. The Social Democrats now have 15 and Sakigake only two.

Hatoyama, a former Sakigake leader and a one-time member of the reformist bloc which ended the LDP's 38-year monopoly on power in 1993, said the Democrats were concerned their voices would be drowned out if they joined an LDP-led ruling bloc with such small numbers. "Fifty-two seats is not enough," he said.
Sakigake looks set to join a Hashimoto-led government, but the Social Democrats -- whose backing is needed for smooth handling of the Upper House especially -- have yet to decide.
Party leader Takako Doi has been cool to the idea, although Upper House members of her party are pushing to join the ruling camp.

Hatoyama also said that a conservative alliance of the LDP and defectors from the biggest opposition party, Shinshinto (the New Frontier Party), could not be ruled out. Shinshinto, which with 156 seats has four fewer than before the election, is thought to be threatened by defections or possibly a split.

Hatoyama said that with more than 50 seats, the Democrats -- ardent advocates of trimming down government and reducing bureaucrats' grip on policy -- would still have the ability to introduce bills into parliament as an opposition party.
He questioned the LDP's commitment to such changes, even though Hashimoto made calls for such "administrative reform" a centrepiece of his campaign.

"What the LDP is calling administrative reform and what we are calling administrative reform are different things," he said. "Take mountain-climbing for example. It is a different matter to tackle a 500-metre mountain than to conquer an 8,000-metre peak."

He reiterated his party's support for a planned rise in the nation's consumption tax from three to five percent from next April, and said some extra budget for the current fiscal year to the end of March would be needed.

But he cast doubt on the advisability of crafting a five trillion yen ($44.6 billion) budget including three trillion yen ($26.7 billion) of public works spending, given Japan's huge budget deficit and doubts about the stimulative impact of such spending. Ahead of the election, some LDP officials called for such a budget.

Hatoyama said that from the Democrats' perspective, the best outcome of the political muddle would be for the LDP to form a stand-alone government. "Then we would support those policies we thought right and oppose those we didn't," he said.
Hashimoto wants to work out the shape of his government by early November so parliament can convene on November 7 to formally reappoint the prime minister. ($1=112 yen)
